newsitem.title: UK: FOCUS-Euro shares slide, dollar weak versus mark.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Euro shares slide, dollar weak versus mark.

text.p: European stock markets went into a steep slide in early business on Monday, taking their cue from Wall Street's second biggest points loss in history on Friday.
However, shares recovered from their lows amid uncertainty over whether the drop marked an end to a relentless rise in U.S. and European share prices or just a short-term correction.

The dollar was weaker against the mark as currency markets fretted over the possibility of higher German interest rates in a week that holds key meetings of monetary policy makers in both the United States and Germany.

Gold, meanwhile, added a couple of dollars on bullion market hopes that stock market woes could send some funds its way but dealers said investors still seemed to lack trust in precious metals as safe havens.
A weak dollar and worries about U.S. profits wiped 247.37 points, or more than three percent, off the Dow Jones Industrial Average to 7,694.66 on Friday.

Wall Street's fall spurred heavy selling on Monday on Asian markets, many of which are also being undermined by currency turmoil in the region. Tokyo's 225-share Nikkei average in Tokyo fell 1.47 percent.

Continental European markets, several closed on Friday for a holiday, were generally hit more than London, Europe's largest stock market, which had already responded to the early stages of Friday's Dow plunge.

But London still had a tough start to the week, with the FTSE 100 index of blue chips opening with a loss of nearly 1.5 percent and extending this before reviving to a deficit of almost one percent in mid-morning.

The FTSE had tumbled 125.5 points or 2.5 percent on Friday, its largest loss in percentage terms in five years -- but compared with a much larger plunge of 250.7 points, or 12.22 percent, in the "crash" of October 20, 1987.
Analysts said Monday's initial sell-off might prompt some caution, at least until Wall Street reopened, as the U.S. bond market was more resilient.

"I think what will happen is that the market-makers will mark it down quickly, and then there will be a pause for the investor reaction and that will determine the next move," Richard Jeffrey, head of research at Charterhouse Tilney, said.

German shares dropped sharply in pre-bourse electronic trading and by mid-morning the IBIS DAX index was down around 1.6 percent but above its lows. In Frankfurt floor trade the DAX index showed a fall of more than 3.5 percent but it had closed on Friday before Wall Street's retreat.

Paris, one of a number of markets closed on Friday for Assumption Day, was particularly hard hit with the CAC-40 down down more than three percent at one stage before staging a mini-revival. Italian, Spanish and Austrian stocks all lost more than 2.5 percent at the opening.
On foreign exchange markets, the dollar was unsettled by jitters about German interest rates before the Bundesbank holds its first meeting on Thursday after the summer break.
It managed to hold just above 1.81 marks but this was some eight pfennigs below a near-eight year peak of 1.8913 hit early this month.
"Sentiment is still fragile ahead of Tuesday's German repo tender and the Bundesbank council meeting on Thursday," said Mark Geddes, treasury economist at ABN AMRO.

Economists doubt whether the German central bank would move towards higher rates at the tender or tighten credit after the council meeting since remarks showing German officials' concern about the mark's decline and inflation had already made an impact.

"We continue to look for unchanged interest rates in Germany near-term, not least since the interest rate threat from the Bundesbank has provided a welcome correction in dollar/mark and restored some order to price action in the mark," said Michael Lewis, international economist at Deutsche Morgan Grenfell.

Markets are also awaiting news from the U.S. Federal Open Market Committee, the central bank's policy-making arm, which meets to consider interest rates on Tuesday but is not generally expected by economists to raise U.S. rates just yet.

A rally in the dollar/yen rate, meanwhile, was capped by remarks from U.S. Deputy Trade Representative Jeffrey Lang who expressed concern about Japanese trade data. Japan's customs-cleared trade surplus jumped almost 70 percent in July.
CURRENCIES AT 0930 GMT
The dollar was quoted around 1.8105 marks and 117.45 yen, compared with 1.8227 and 117.76 in late European trading on Friday.
STOCK MARKETS AT 0930 GMT
LONDON - The FTSE 100 index was down 44.3 points or 0.91 percent at 4,821.5.
FRANKFURT - The DAX index for floor trade was 145.82 points or 3.51 percent lower at 4,007.4. The IBIS index for electronic trade was down 66.48 points or 1.63 percent at 4,011.11.
PARIS - The CAC-40 index was 62.11 points or 2.13 percent lower at 2,859.73.
The Madrid stock market was down around 2.30 percent, Milan just over two percent, Stockholm just over one percent and Zurich 2.2 percent.
PRECIOUS METALS
Gold was fixed at $326.05 an ounce, up from Friday's London close of $324.35. Silver gained eight cents to $4.53.
